instrument: Treaty of Fort Stanwix, Oct. 22, 1784
summary: Article I required the four nations treated as defeated British allies to hand over six hostages, held by the US until all captives were returned. The cession in Art. III was signed while those hostages were in US custody. The Six Nations council later repudiated the delegates' authority (see atlas V003).
verbatim_quote: Six hostages shall be immediately delivered to the commissioners by the said nations
federal_account_contrast: Kappler/Royce present the cession as a peace treaty. The text itself makes peace conditional on hostage delivery, so consent was given under a hostage regime.
map_implication: Flag the 1784 Stanwix cession polygon with HOSTAGE and DURESS badges; link to V003 (council repudiation).
notes: Quote matches several transcriptions (Avalon, Groningen, Dillon 1858). Royce area number to be taken from atlas Royce join; not checked here.

source_doc: Yale Avalon Project, Treaty with the Wyandot etc. 1785 https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/wya1785.asp; Shawnee Nation mukurtu transcript https://mukurtu.scit-nsn.gov/system/files/atoms/file/1785%20Treaty%20of%20Ft.%20McIntosh%20transcript.docx; OSU 7 Stat. 16 record
instrument: Treaty of Fort McIntosh, Jan. 21, 1785
summary: Article I required three chiefs (one Wyandot, two Delaware) to be delivered to US commissioners as hostages until all prisoners were returned. The same instrument drew a boundary ceding most of present Ohio east and south of the line. A catalog note says the treaty was never carried into effect.
verbatim_quote: Three chiefs, one from among the Wiandot, and two from among the Delaware nations, shall be delivered up to the Commissioners of the United States
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows Fort McIntosh as a cession; the instrument was a 'conquest theory' dictation with hostages, and the western confederacy (Shawnee, Miami) was not party.
map_implication: Badge the Fort McIntosh cession HOSTAGE; note 'never carried into effect' and supersession by Fort Harmar 1789 and Greenville 1795.
notes: The Shawnee Tribe hosts a transcript on its Mukurtu archive, a Native-curated source.

source_doc: Yale Avalon Project, Treaty with the Shawnee 1786 https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/shaw1786.asp; OSU treaty 0016; summaries of Kekewepelethy / Fort Finney (Wikipedia, NKY Tribune https://nkytribune.com/?p=171759)
place: Fort Finney, mouth of the Great Miami River (near North Bend, Ohio) 39.13,-84.80
instrument: Treaty of Fort Finney (Treaty with the Shawnee), Jan. 31, 1786
summary: Article I required the Shawnee to deliver three hostages to be held until all prisoners were returned. When Kekewepelethy offered black wampum signalling refusal, George Rogers Clark knocked it to the floor and ground it under his boot, and the commissioners threatened war. Moluntha's group signed.
federal_account_contrast: Kappler records a treaty of peace and acknowledgment; the negotiating record shows refusal answered by threat, plus a hostage clause.
map_implication: Badge the 1786 Shawnee instrument HOSTAGE and DURESS_MILITARY.
notes: Article I text confirmed via search snippets of Avalon/OSU, paraphrased here because exact wording not captured. The wampum episode rests on secondary accounts of Butler's journal; Butler and Parsons/Clark named variously.

source_doc: Fort Finney summaries (Wikipedia 'Fort Finney (Ohio)', 'Kekewepelethy', NKY Tribune https://nkytribune.com/?p=171759)
instrument: Treaty of Fort Finney, Jan. 31, 1786
summary: Only about a third of the Shawnee attended; the treaty was reluctantly signed by Moluntha's people and renounced by other Shawnee leaders, and the Northwest Indian War followed.
verbatim_quote: reluctantly signed by the Shawnees and later renounced by other Shawnee leaders
federal_account_contrast: Presented as binding on the Shawnee nation; most Shawnee were absent and rejected it.
map_implication: Mark instrument as minority-signed / repudiated.
notes: Quote is from a search-returned secondary summary; check against Colin Calloway, The Shawnees and the War for America (2007).

source_doc: Yale Avalon Project, Treaty with the Wyandot etc. 1789 https://avalon.law.yale.edu/18th_century/wya1789.asp; War Department Papers https://wardepartmentpapers.org/document/39741/

instrument: Treaty of Fort Harmar (with the Wyandot etc.), Jan. 9, 1789
summary: Article I required the nations to deliver two Wyandot persons as hostages to Governor St. Clair, held until prisoners were restored. The treaty re-confirmed the Fort McIntosh line, and the Shawnee and Miami, who were fighting the US, were not party.
federal_account_contrast: Treated as a confirmation of 1785; it again rested on hostages and excluded the nations actually resisting.
map_implication: Badge HOSTAGE; note Shawnee/Miami not party.
notes: Hostage clause confirmed in Avalon via search snippet; Shawnee/Miami absence is standard scholarship but not re-verified this session.

map_implication: Badge Greenville cession HOSTAGE and DURESS_MILITARY.

source_doc: G. A. Custer, My Life on the Plains (1874), as excerpted via Kansas Collection https://kancoll.org/books/custerg/cgchap14.htm; Find a Grave summaries; PSL TREC context
instrument: Implementation of the Treaty of Medicine Lodge with the Kiowa and Comanche, Oct. 21, 1867
summary: After Washita, Custer seized Kiowa chiefs Satanta and Lone Wolf, who had come in under a flag of truce, and Sheridan ordered them hanged if their bands did not come in to Fort Cobb. The Kiowa moved onto the Medicine Lodge reservation under this threat; the chiefs were released about February 1869.
verbatim_quote: I then arrested both him and Lone Wolf and held them as hostages
federal_account_contrast: The federal record treats Kiowa settlement on the reservation as performance of a consensual treaty; it was compelled by hostage-taking with a death threat.
map_implication: On the KCA reservation polygon, add a 1868-69 event: 'reservation occupation compelled by hostage-taking of Satanta and Lone Wolf'.
notes: Quote is Custer's own memoir. Sources differ on whether Custer or Sheridan issued the hanging order. Agency affidavits later showed both chiefs slept at Fort Cobb on Nov. 27, 1868, i.e., they were not at Washita.

source_doc: Washita summaries: ICT 'Custer attacks peaceful Cheyenne' https://ictnews.org/archive/native-history-custer-attacks-peaceful-cheyenne-in-oklahoma/; Indy Rep News 'Stockade of Infamy' https://www.indyrepnews.com/article/opinions/stockade-infamy; World History Encyclopedia https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2550/
place: Washita River near Cheyenne, Oklahoma 35.62,-99.70; Fort Hays, Kansas 38.86,-99.34
instrument: Treaty of Medicine Lodge with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 28, 1867 (implementation)
summary: Custer's troops took 53 Cheyenne women and children captive at Washita and later held them in a stockade at Fort Hays. Sheridan's winter campaign orders called for capturing women and children, and historians describe the captives as hostages and human shields used while bands were driven onto the reservation.
federal_account_contrast: Royce/Kappler show Medicine Lodge as a consensual exchange; Cheyenne reservation settlement in 1869 occurred with families held captive.
map_implication: Add Washita and Fort Hays as linked event points on the Medicine Lodge Cheyenne-Arapaho reservation layer, tagged HOSTAGE (women and children).
notes: Search did not find a source tying the Fort Hays captives to an explicit surrender demand; the leverage claim is historians' interpretation. Black Kettle was a Medicine Lodge signatory (see WEB-DUR row on Washita massacre).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024
place: Sweetwater Creek, Texas Panhandle; Fort Hays, Kansas
instrument: Medicine Lodge (Cheyenne-Arapaho) 1867, implementation
summary: On the Sweetwater, Custer took three Cheyenne chiefs hostage and threatened to hang them to force release of two white women captives; the chiefs were sent to Fort Hays, where two were killed 'attempting to escape'.
verbatim_quote: Custer took Cheyenne chiefs Big Head, Dull Knife (Lean Face), and Fat Bear hostage, using the threat of hanging them
federal_account_contrast: Absent from treaty-based maps; shows that leadership available to consent was held or killed.
map_implication: Event point on Sweetwater Creek linked to the Cheyenne-Arapaho reservation.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (quoting secondary history)
place: Blue Water Creek (Ash Hollow), Nebraska 41.29,-102.13; Fort Pierre, South Dakota
instrument: Harney council at Fort Pierre, March 1856 (unratified 'treaty')
summary: Gen. William Harney attacked Little Thunder's Brule camp, killing about 86 men, women and children and taking about 70 hostages (mostly women and children). Harney then dictated terms to Lakota bands at Fort Pierre in 1856 while captives were held.
verbatim_quote: He killed eighty-six men women, and children and took seventy hostages
federal_account_contrast: No treaty polygon reflects this; it shaped later Lakota dealings and the 1851 Fort Laramie aftermath.

source_doc: Minnesota Historical Society, 'Forced Marches & Imprisonment' https://www.mnhs.org/usdakotawar/stories/history/aftermath/forced-marches-imprisonment; MNopedia https://mnopedia.org/node/15662; MNHS Fort Snelling page
place: Fort Snelling internment camp, Bdote (Minneapolis-St. Paul) 44.89,-93.18
instrument: Act of Feb. 16, 1863 (annulling Dakota treaties) and Act of Mar. 3, 1863 (removal)
summary: About 1,600-1,700 Dakota non-combatants, mostly women, children and elders, were held over the winter in a stockade below Fort Snelling, where 130-300 died. While they were held, Congress annulled all Dakota treaties and forfeited their remaining Minnesota lands and annuities, then removed survivors to Crow Creek in May 1863.
verbatim_quote: twelve-foot tall wooden stockade
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows Dakota land as ceded by the 1851 treaties; the remaining reservation was taken by statute without consent, with families confined.
map_implication: Recolor the 1858 Dakota reservation strip on the Minnesota River as TAKEN_WITHOUT_CONSENT (1863 Act); add Fort Snelling camp point.
notes: This was confinement rather than hostage-taking tied to a signing; categorized HOSTAGE per task scope (women and children held). SD legislative resolutions state the 1863 acts remain unrepealed.

source_doc: Smithsonian NMAI blog https://www.smithsonianmag.com/blogs/national-museum-american-indian/2018/02/22/treaty-that-reversed-a-removal-navajo-treaty-1868-goes-on-view/; Zinn Ed Project https://www.zinnedproject.org/news/tdih/navajo-treaty-of-1868/
place: Fort Sumner / Bosque Redondo, New Mexico 34.40,-104.19

summary: The treaty was signed by Dine leaders held with about 8,000-10,000 people at Bosque Redondo, where up to about 3,500 died of starvation, disease and executions over four years. Sherman's first proposal was removal to Indian Territory; return home was the price of signing a cession of most of Dinetah.
verbatim_quote: bringing us here has made many of us die, also a great number of our animals
federal_account_contrast: Atlas V040/V041 treat the 1868 treaty's later breaches; the signing itself occurred in captivity.
map_implication: Tag the 1868 Navajo cession as signed by an interned population (DURESS_STARVATION); show Long Walk routes.
notes: Barboncito's words are from the 1868 council proceedings as quoted in secondary sources. The often-cited 'I hope to God...' line was not verified.

verbatim_quote: General Miles had promised that we might return to our own country with what stock we had left
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the Wallowa as ceded in 1863; non-signers who resisted were imprisoned and exiled.
map_implication: Link Wallowa (1855 reservation portion) to 'never consented, taken via 1863 minority treaty and 1877 war'.

source_doc: ABA Journal 'Congress passes the Sell or Starve Act' https://abajournal.com/magazine/article/congress-passes-the-sell-or-starve-act; United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980); littlebighorn.info text of 1876 agreement

place: Great Sioux Reservation incl. He Sapa (Black Hills); councils at Red Cloud and Spotted Tail agencies

summary: The 1876 appropriation barred any further subsistence for the Sioux until they relinquished the Black Hills and hunting rights. The Manypenny commission then presented the cession to bands dependent on rations, and Congress enacted it in 1877.
verbatim_quote: halting any aid to the Sioux until they relinquished both their hunting rights and their claim to the Black Hills
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows the Black Hills as ceded by agreement; the Supreme Court held the 1877 Act a taking; the agreement was extracted by a starvation statute.

source_doc: United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980) syllabus (via LOC https://www.loc.gov/item/usrep448371 and summaries); case brief pastpaperhero
instrument: Manypenny agreement 1876 vs. Fort Laramie Treaty 1868 Art. 12
summary: Art. 12 of the 1868 treaty required signatures of three-fourths of adult males for any cession; the 1876 paper was signed by about 10 percent. The Court of Claims and ICC found a want of fair and honorable dealings; the Court awarded money, not land.
verbatim_quote: signed by only 10% of Sioux adult males
federal_account_contrast: Royce schedule treats the 1877 Act as the cession instrument without noting the 3/4 rule.
map_implication: Display 'signed by ~10% vs 75% required' on the 1877 polygon.
notes: '10%' is from a case-brief summary; the opinion itself discusses signatures by chiefs and headmen only. The phrase 'ripe and rank case of dishonorable dealings' (Court of Claims 1975, quoted in 448 U.S.) was not verified this session.

source_doc: NPS 'Treaty of Fort Jackson' https://www.nps.gov/articles/treaty-of-fort-jackson.htm; Encyclopedia of Alabama https://encyclopediaofalabama.org/article/h-3026

instrument: Treaty of Fort Jackson, Aug. 9, 1814
summary: Styled a capitulation, the treaty was made with the Creek National Council, a US ally; the Red Sticks who fought were largely dead or in Florida. Jackson took about 21-23 million acres from both factions as payment for the war.
verbatim_quote: unprovoked, inhuman, and sanguinary
federal_account_contrast: Kappler/Royce present a cession by the Creek Nation; the signers were allies punished for a war they fought on the US side.
map_implication: Badge Fort Jackson cession DURESS_MILITARY and 'cession taken from allies'.
notes: Quote is the treaty preamble language as quoted by NPS (Jackson's justification). Acreage varies by source (21 to 23 million). Also ceded Cherokee-claimed land; see Cherokee protests 1816.

federal_account_contrast: Kappler prints the treaty; the side agreement that consumed the cash is invisible on the map.
map_implication: Annotate Royce Dakota 1851 cession with 'treaty money diverted by unread traders' paper'.

source_doc: Wikipedia '1837 Ho-Chunk treaty' (via search); Sauk County Historical Society, Yellow Thunder https://www.saukcountyhistory.org/yellow-thunder/; Annals of Iowa (Simon Cameron Commission) https://pubs.lib.uiowa.edu/annals-of-iowa/article/7288/galley/116025/view
